newsitem.title: UK: UK oil industry not "happy" with cut in tax relief.
newsitem.headline: UK oil industry not "happy" with cut in tax relief.

text.p: Britain's oil drilling industry was disappointed by news that Chancellor Kenneth Clarke wants to withdraw the 100 percent corporation tax deduction for the intangible costs of drilling most oil wells.
But lobby groups and exploration firms said it was too early to say to what extent the proposals would affect North Sea drilling activity.
"Any organisation that loses the ability to write off a tax isn't going to be happy with it," said a spokesman for the UK Offshore Operators Association (UKOOA).
"Clearly our industry needs time to work out the effect this will have on drilling activity and costs," he added.
But a spokesman for a major operator, who declined to be named, said the impact on activity of both proposals was likely to be fairly limited.
The Inland Revenue said in a statement it expected the proposed tax changes would yield 150 million stg in 1998-99 and 200 million stg in 1999-2000. The yield is likely to be less in following years.
The Chancellor also proposed to cut the capital allowance for plant and machinery with a life of more than 25 years to six percent on a reducing balance basis.
This was another matter that looked unfavourable at first sight, but needed closer study, the UKOOA spokesman said.
"It is too early for us to be precise," he said.
He added that his organisation was pleased that the British government had decided to leave major taxes such as the petroleum revenue tax and royalty tax unchanged.
"We are happy that the macro fiscal element of offshore taxation has not been changed and for that we are grateful," the spokesman said.
